title: How MSPs Can Operationalize Agentic AI Governance Across Multiple Tenants
summary: Agentic AI is outpacing governance at every client. Here’s how MSPs turn agent visibility, ownership, and recovery into a recurring revenue service.
body_markdown:
Managed service providers (MSPs) turn agentic AI governance into recurring revenue by packaging the ongoing work AI agents demand, discovery, ownership assignment, data-access mapping, lifecycle recertification, cost oversight, and recovery into a subscription service. Because agents change constantly, this oversight cannot be a one-time project; it becomes a standing managed service billed monthly, not a single engagement.


## Key Takeaways


- **Agentic AI governance is a recurring, not one-time, service opportunity.** Agents are added, changed, and retired continuously, so the oversight work renews every month the same way patching and backup do, giving MSPs a subscription hook instead of a single project fee.
- **Six operational gaps define the service.** Every client deploying agents faces the same six problems: Nobody can see every agent, nobody owns each one, nobody knows what data it touches, nobody retires it when it’s done, nobody tracks what it costs, and nobody can undo what it breaks.
- **Governance, not tooling, is the top-cited barrier to AI adoption among MSP customers.** Research from AvePoint and Omdia found 51% of MSPs point to governance and compliance as the leading obstacle keeping their customers from scaling AI, ahead of security, budget, or skills gaps.
- **Most MSPs are automating around AI readiness, but few have matured into it.** The same research found 94% of MSPs are committed to automating AI data readiness and compliance work, yet only 43% have reached high delivery maturity, leaving a wide operational gap for MSPs willing to close it first.
- **The global AI services partner opportunity is measured in the hundreds of billions.** Omdia forecasts the AI services partner opportunity, spanning data preparation, governance, integration, and operational oversight, will reach US$276 billion by 2030, and governance as a service is one of the fastest-growing slices of that number.
- **This spans Microsoft 365 and every other SaaS platform clients run agents on.** Agents now run inside Microsoft 365 Copilot Studio and SharePoint, but also inside Google Workspace, Salesforce, and other cloud platforms, so an MSP practice built around one vendor’s agent ecosystem will miss most of a client’s real exposure.
- **Recovery is the gap most governance-only offerings skip.** Discovery and policy enforcement tell a client what an agent is doing; only a backup-and-recovery capability lets them undo it when an agent deletes, corrupts, or misconfigures something it shouldn’t have touched.


## Why Does Agentic AI Governance Matter for MSPs Right Now?


Agentic AI governance is the ongoing discovery, ownership, access mapping, lifecycle management, cost control, and recovery capability an organization needs to run AI agents safely. It matters for MSPs now because agent adoption is outpacing governance maturity inside their client base, and every ungoverned agent is a support ticket, an audit finding, or a breach waiting to surface.


Agents are software that plans, decides, and takes multistep action across systems with limited or no human approval at each step, not software that simply answers a prompt and stops. That distinction is why agents create a governance problem traditional AI policy was never written for: A chatbot can say something wrong, but an agent can delete a file, grant an access request, or send an email on its own.


Adoption is already well past the experimentation stage.[According to BCG](https://www.bcg.com/publications/2025/machines-that-manage-themselves) , 35% percent of organizations have begun using agentic AI, and another 44% plan to soon.[McKinsey’s State of AI research](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai-2025) also found that 62% of organizations are at least experimenting with AI agent though no single business function has scaled agents past 10% penetration yet. That gap between rapid adoption and thin oversight is precisely where an MSP’s governance practice fits.


Consider a 200-person professional services firm. A single department can stand up a dozen Copilot Studio or Salesforce Agentforce agents in an afternoon, without IT ever approving a request or logging what each agent can access. Multiply that across every department and every client an MSP serves, and the governance gap isn’t hypothetical; it’s already sitting inside most tenants an MSP manages today.


> The challenge for MSPs isn’t governing a single environment. It’s delivering consistent visibility, ownership, policy enforcement, and reporting across dozens or hundreds of client tenants. As AI adoption accelerates, multitenant management becomes critical to scaling governance effectively.


For a deeper technical walkthrough of agentic AI governance itself, see[AvePoint’s The Definitive Guide to Agentic AI Governance: Securing a New Era of Autonomous AI](https://www.avepoint.com/blog/strategy-blog/definitive-guide-agentic-ai-governance-security-autonomous-systems) . The rest of this article focuses specifically on how MSPs turn that governance work into a priced, recurring offer.


The barrier holding most organizations back isn’t a lack of interest in AI agents; it’s governance maturity.[Research from AvePoint and Omdia](https://www.avepoint.com/news/research-from-avepoint-and-omdia-reveals-governance-and-compliance-as-the-leading-ai-adoption-barrier-among-ms-ps-260409) found that 51% of MSPs cite governance and compliance as the leading barrier keeping their customers from scaling AI, ahead of data and security management, value realization, or technical expertise gaps. That’s the opening: The obstacle to AI adoption is exactly the service an MSP is positioned to sell.


## The Six Governance Gaps Every Client Creates When It Deploys AI Agents


Every organization running AI agents runs into the same six operational gaps, whether it has three agents or three hundred. Each gap on its own is a support and compliance risk; together, they are the service catalog for an MSP’s agentic AI governance practice.


### Why Don’t Organizations Have Visibility Into Every AI Agent They’ve Deployed?


Organizations lack agent visibility because agents are created inside individual SaaS tools, Copilot Studio, Salesforce Agentforce, and Google Vertex AI, by business users without a central request or approval process. Without an inventory that spans every platform, IT cannot answer a basic audit question: How many agents exist, and what can each one do?


This isn’t a hypothetical gap. Up to[one in five organizations](https://www.avepoint.com/shifthappens/reports/artificial-intelligence-report-2026) do not know whether employees are using unsanctioned AI tools. For generative AI (GenAI), that figure has nearly tripled since 2025. While both sanctioned and unsanctioned access to agent-creation tools grew year over year, shadow AI is expanding faster than visibility. A policy nobody can find is functionally the same as no policy at all, and an inventory is the only way to know what that missing policy should actually govern.


### Who Is Responsible When an AI Agent Makes a Mistake?


Ownership is unclear because most agents are built by a business team, not IT, and no one is formally accountable for what the agent does once it’s live. An agent built by a marketing analyst to draft customer emails can quietly outlive the analyst’s own awareness of what it was ever supposed to do.


Without a named owner, an agent has no one to answer for its permissions, its behavior, or its eventual retirement. That’s a governance gap with a direct fix: assigning ownership at the moment an agent is discovered, and reviewing that ownership on a fixed cadence rather than assuming it will surface itself.


### What Data Can Each AI Agent Actually Access?


Most organizations cannot answer this question for every agent they run, because agent permissions are granted at setup and rarely reviewed again. An agent built to summarize one SharePoint library often inherits far broader access than the single task it was built for actually requires.


[AvePoint’s State of AI in 2026 research](https://www.avepoint.com/shifthappens/reports/artificial-intelligence-report-2026) found that 89.5% of organizations suffered a GenAI breach and 88.4% suffered an AI agent breach in the past year. With oversharing permissions, an agent or user can access data that should never be touched, which is among the leading causes of data breaches. Mapping data access per agent, not just per user, is what closes this specific gap.


### How Should MSPs Manage an AI Agent’s Lifecycle, From Deployment to Retirement?


An agent’s lifecycle runs from provisioning through periodic recertification to retirement, and most organizations only handle the first step. Agents built for a since-completed project, or by an employee who has since left, routinely keep running with no one reviewing whether they still should.


[Gartner predicts](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-06-25-gartner-predicts-over-40-percent-of-agentic-ai-projects-will-be-canceled-by-end-of-2027) more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 due to escalating costs, unclear business value, and inadequate risk controls. A recertification cadence, checking on a fixed schedule whether an agent still has an owner, still needs its access, and is still in active use, is built specifically to catch a project before it becomes one of that 40%.


### Who Is Tracking What AI Agents Actually Cost?


In most organizations, no one is, because agent spend is spread across per-seat licenses, token consumption, and infrastructure costs that never appear on a single invoice. Agent sprawl compounds this: Agents built for a finished project often keep consuming licenses and compute long after anyone is using them.


A client running agents across several departments, each provisioned independently, can accumulate meaningful monthly spend that no single budget owner ever reviews. Cost governance closes this gap by giving a client pay-as-you-go visibility into what each agent actually costs, paired with budget guardrails before spend becomes a surprise on next quarter’s bill.


### What Happens When an AI Agent Deletes, Corrupts, or Misconfigures Data?


In most environments, nothing purpose-built exists for this. Agent actions are treated like any other change, with no dedicated way to roll back a bad update, a wrongful deletion, or a misconfigured workflow the agent applied on its own.


Discovery and policy tools tell a client what an agent is doing; they generally stop short of undoing what it already did. A recovery capability that protects an agent’s own topics, prompts, and orchestration logic, not just the data it touched, is what lets a client roll back an agent’s mistake instead of rebuilding it from scratch.


## How Do MSPs Turn These Six Gaps Into a Recurring Revenue Service?


MSPs turn agentic AI governance into recurring revenue by tiering it like any other managed service: a foundational tier for discovery and reporting, a managed tier that adds ownership and access enforcement, and an advanced tier that adds cost governance and agent recovery. Each tier is billed monthly and scoped to a client’s agent count and risk profile, not delivered as a one-time audit.


The six gaps above map directly onto a repeatable delivery motion. Each step below builds on the one before it, and each one is a natural point to introduce a higher service tier rather than a one-time add-on fee:


- **Run the initial agent discovery and inventory.** Scan every platform a client runs, not just Microsoft 365, and produce a baseline count of every agent, sanctioned or shadow.
- **Assign ownership and set the recertification cadence.** Every agent gets a named owner and a review date; agents without one are flagged for immediate follow-up.
- **Map data access per agent and close the obvious gaps.** Identify which agents can reach sensitive or regulated data, and right-size access down to what each agent’s task actually requires.
- **Enforce policy and cost guardrails continuously.** Move from a point-in-time report to standing enforcement: Policy violations and cost overages get flagged as they happen, not at the next audit.
- **Add agent backup and recovery as the top-tier offer.** Package the ability to roll back an agent’s configuration after an unwanted change as the premium tier, since it’s the capability most governance-only competitors don’t offer at all.
- **Report the evidence back to the client every cycle.** Turn each cycle’s findings into the audit-ready evidence a client’s own compliance or board reporting needs, which is what justifies the subscription renewing.

## What Mistakes Should MSPs Avoid When Building an Agentic AI Governance Practice?


The most common mistake is treating agentic AI governance as a one-time audit instead of a standing service, which throws away the recurring revenue opportunity entirely. The fixes below are what keep the practice priced and delivered as a subscription rather than a project.


- **Scoping the practice to Microsoft 365 only.** Agents increasingly run inside Google Workspace, Salesforce, and other SaaS platforms; a Microsoft-only practice misses most of a client’s real exposure.
- **Selling governance without a recovery story.** Discovery and policy reporting alone don’t answer a client’s hardest question: What happens when an agent breaks something? Without a recovery capability, the offer is incomplete.
- **Skipping the recertification cadence.** A discovery scan that’s never repeated is a snapshot, not governance; agents added the following month go right back to being invisible.
- **Underpricing governance as a free bundled extra.** Folding agent governance into an existing support contract at no additional charge signals it has no value; price it as its own line item from the start.
- **Leading with compliance jargon instead of a concrete finding.** Terms like AI cloud security posture management or model risk mean little to a first-time buyer; a specific finding, such as an unowned agent with access to payroll data, sells the service far faster.


## How Does Agentic AI Governance Work Across Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, and Salesforce?


Agentic AI governance has to span every platform a client runs agents on, not just Microsoft 365, because agents are proliferating inside Google Workspace and Salesforce at the same pace. A practice scoped to one vendor’s ecosystem will miss agents that most business users never think to mention.


Microsoft 365 is usually where agent sprawl shows up first, since Copilot Studio, Microsoft Foundry, and SharePoint agents make it simple for a business user to stand up an agent without a formal IT request. But the same dynamic is playing out on Google Cloud, where Vertex AI agents are proliferating inside Google Workspace-heavy organizations, and inside Salesforce, where Agentforce agents are built directly by sales and service teams.

For an MSP, the practical takeaway is the same regardless of which vendor’s tools a client standardizes on: The governance service has to follow the agent, not stop at the boundary of one platform.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What counts as an AI agent, versus a chatbot or a simple AI-powered feature?


An AI agent is software that can plan, decide, and take multistep action across systems with limited or no human approval at each step, not just respond to a single prompt. Gartner defines agentic AI as autonomous or semi-autonomous software that perceives context, decides, and acts to reach a goal, while McKinsey adds that an agent adapts its own next step based on the outcome of the last one. A chatbot or a simple AI-powered feature, by contrast, answers a question or completes one discrete task and stops; it doesn’t orchestrate a workflow across multiple tools or make a follow-on decision on its own. This distinction matters for governance because an agent’s ability to act, not just respond, is exactly what creates the visibility, ownership, and data-access exposure this article covers.


### What is the difference between agentic AI governance and traditional AI governance?


Traditional AI governance typically covers model risk: how a model was trained, whether its outputs are biased, and whether it complies with a specific regulation. Agentic AI governance adds an operational layer on top of that: which agents exist, who owns each one, what data and systems each agent can reach, and what happens when an agent takes an action nobody approved. Model-level governance asks whether the AI is fair and accurate; agentic governance asks whether the AI, once it starts acting on its own, can be tracked, contained, and rolled back. MSPs building a governance practice need both, but agent-specific oversight is the newer, faster-growing gap, since most organizations’ existing AI policies were written before agents could act across systems at all.


### How do MSPs typically price an agentic AI governance service?


Most MSPs price agentic AI governance the same way they price other managed services: a recurring monthly fee scoped to agent count, data footprint, or client risk tier, rather than a flat one-time project fee. Common models blend a base subscription for discovery and reporting with add-on pricing for higher tiers, such as active policy enforcement, cost governance, or agent backup and recovery. Because agent counts change constantly as clients add and retire agents, usage-based or tiered pricing tracks the real workload better than a fixed annual contract does. The right model depends on a client’s agent maturity: A client with three agents and no formal AI policy is a different service, and a different price, than one running dozens of agents across multiple departments.


### What does agentic AI governance mean specifically for Microsoft 365 customers?


For Microsoft 365 customers, agentic AI governance means extending oversight to every agent built inside Copilot Studio, SharePoint agents, and Microsoft Foundry, not just the Copilot licenses IT already tracks. Microsoft 365 makes agent creation easy for business users, which is exactly why shadow agents proliferate there first: A department can stand up a Copilot Studio agent without a formal IT request. An MSP serving Microsoft 365-heavy clients still needs a plan for the rest of a client’s SaaS estate, since agents increasingly run inside Google Workspace and Salesforce as well, and a Microsoft-only governance practice will miss that exposure entirely.


### How does AI agent adoption change an MSP’s existing backup and security services?


AI agent adoption adds a new category of asset that existing backup and security services typically don’t cover: the agent’s own configuration, prompts, and orchestration logic, not just the data it touches. A client’s existing Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace backup protects mailboxes, files, and sites, but it generally has no purpose-built way to restore an agent’s settings after the agent itself makes an unwanted change or gets misconfigured. Security services face a similar gap: Existing identity and access reviews weren’t built to ask whether an agent, not a person, has access it shouldn’t. MSPs extending their backup and security practices to cover agents directly are addressing a gap their current service catalog simply doesn’t reach yet.


### How often should an MSP recertify a client’s AI agents?


A quarterly recertification cadence is a reasonable default for most clients, checking that every agent still has an active owner, still needs the data access it was granted, and is still in active use. Higher-risk agents, ones with access to regulated or highly sensitive data, or ones making decisions with limited human review, warrant a shorter cycle, such as monthly. The right cadence should track a client’s own audit and compliance calendar rather than a fixed industry number, since a client under active regulatory scrutiny needs more frequent evidence than one that isn’t. Whatever the cadence, it needs to be a standing, scheduled activity, not a one-time check performed when an agent is first deployed.


### What is the difference between AI agent governance and AI agent management?


AI agent management generally refers to the technical work of deploying, configuring, and maintaining agents, keeping them running, updated, and integrated with the tools they need. AI agent governance is the oversight layer on top of that: assigning ownership, reviewing data access, enforcing policy, and producing the audit evidence that proves an organization’s agents are under control. A client can have strong agent management, agents that run reliably, and still have weak agent governance, no one accountable for what those agents are allowed to do. MSPs building a recurring-revenue practice around agents need to be clear with clients about which of the two, or both, they’re actually selling.


### How should an MSP get started with agentic AI governance if no clients are using AI agents yet?


Start with a no-cost discovery scan on an existing client’s Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace tenant. Most organizations already have more agents running than IT is aware of, since Copilot Studio and similar tools let business users create agents without a formal request, so the discovery step alone usually surfaces a concrete finding to bring back to the client. Use that finding to open a conversation about ownership and policy, rather than leading with a sales pitch for a governance product the client doesn’t yet see the need for. Building the practice on one or two early clients, then packaging what’s repeatable into a standard service tier, is a lower-risk path than building a full three-tier offering before a single client has bought it.


### Why is multitenant management important for AI governance?


Multitenant management helps MSPs deliver consistent governance across multiple customer environments. As clients deploy more AI agents, manually managing visibility, ownership, policy enforcement, and reporting tenant by tenant becomes operationally difficult. A multitenant approach allows MSPs to standardize governance controls, improve operational efficiency, and scale service delivery across their customer base.


### What is an AI Trust Layer, and why does it matter for MSPs?


An AI Trust Layer is a unifying set of controls across an organization’s people, data, apps, and AI agents that makes AI adoption defensible: provable to an auditor, a regulator, or an executive that AI is being used safely. It matters for MSPs because it reframes governance from a list of individual tasks, discovery, policy, backup, into a single outcome a client is willing to pay for on an ongoing basis: confidence that its AI use won’t become tomorrow’s incident or audit finding. Positioning a governance practice around trust, not just compliance, also helps an MSP sell to the business owner and not only the IT buyer, since trust is a board-level concern in a way that a checklist of controls isn’t.
